docs.snippet: Gucci Westman and Guido Palau discuss hair and makeup with the Moment.
docs.lead_paragraph: “It was really embarrassing,” said Revlon’s Global Artistic Director, Gucci Westman, dressed in a tweed aqua blazer, baggy white pants and leopard slippers backstage at Rag & Bone. “My husband (Rag & Bone designer David Neville) called and said, ‘Where are you? We need the turquoise trousers for the show.'” By accident, Westman had selected a look that made it into the final collection, instead of an edit, to wear today, a mistake that was quickly corrected. “It’s the strongest Spring, yet,” she said explaining her excitement at the ’70s surf vacation and 90s rave culture-inspired pieces. She chose a minimal makeup look, so as not to compete with the bright colors of the clothes. Eyes were simply taupe Revlon 16H shadow in Addictive with a touch of Sueded Brow liner. Cheeks were tinted with a light bronzer and blush in Tawny Peach while lips were pale pink, coated with shine and patted with powder. “Personally, I don’t think lip gloss is cool.” What is cool– and consistently Rag & Bone– appears to be grey nails. Jin Soon Choi took last season’s slate to a lighter shade of concrete- Revlon’s Smoky Canvas or Hazy. As for hair, Guido Palau admitted the idea was “effortless,” though the process was anything but. “Eighty percent of the New York designers want ease. It always looks glamorous,” he said. To achieve this, Palau tightly braided the underside of the models’ hair and then added extensions for length to create the illusion of fineness. He then used Redken Satinwear all over damp hair which he dried with a Mason Pearson brush and Sultra tools. The hair was then clamped at the neck with a Velcro strap to create a bob-like effect. Ah, this explains the rave reference.

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Rag & Bone

docs.abstract: Last season’s wig-wrapped hair and black, fringed, pastel falls turned into “effortless glamour” this season.
docs.snippet: Last season’s wig-wrapped hair and black, fringed, pastel falls turned into “effortless glamour” this season.
docs.lead_paragraph: “We usually have a strong beauty concept,” said the stylist Natasha Royt backstage at Mandy Coon. “This time it’s modern, approachable, realistic, low maintenance– cool. We want to let the graphic, modern clothes speak for themselves.” Last season’s wig-wrapped hair and black, fringed, pastel falls turned into “effortless glamour” this season, according to Rolando Beauchamp. Loose waves came by way of Bumble + Bumble Gel, a blow dry, and then a one-inch curling iron wrapped at the shaft of the hair, all set with Bumble + Bumble Grooming Creme and roughed up with BB Texture for a messy, matte finish. The last step ensured that nothing was “too pretty or too shiny.” Coon’s color-blocked looks were translated into Mark Rothko-inspired, multi-step eyes at the hands of the makeup artist Francelle Daly for NARS. Lavender-grey Lhasa was the primary shadow. “I’m obsessed with this shade,” Daly said. “It’s rarely used for spring/summer collections.” She also added a trio of pinks with an icy tone at both corners of the eye. The Rue Bonaparte Larger Than Life Eyeliner pencil, a natural beige, was used to neutralize under the eye while white Santa Monica Boulevard lined inside. Madison Avenue grey was drawn as triangles on the outer edge of the lid. Without mascara on the bottom lashes, this all contributed to a “special effect” accompanied by a raspberry lip. An effect that caused one model to comment, “I look like I’ve been crying.” Her friend countered, “No, you look beautiful.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Mandy Coon

docs.abstract: Andre Rodman and Gregory Arlt discuss hair and makeup with the Moment.
docs.snippet: Andre Rodman and Gregory Arlt discuss hair and makeup with the Moment.
docs.lead_paragraph: Unlike some creatives who choke under pressure, the menswear designer Antonio Azzuolo, a finalist for this year’s CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund, gracefully eased the reins and took a more relaxed approach to his Spring/Summer collection. Mr. Azzuolo explained backstage, “My first collection was very formal, all about suits. This season I designed more liberally, drawing inspiration from Les Minets, a French/British hybrid movement of mod culture. These young men shunned bourgeois culture, but still dressed up. They were rough and rebellious, but chic and sophisticated as well.” Noting the designer’s departure from his norm of neat, the hairstylist Andre Rodman casually styled models’ hair with his hands and a healthy dollop of Shu Uemura Shape Paste, to enhance each guy’s individual hair texture. Mr. Rodman completed looks with a brisk shake of the dryer, along with “lots of Oribe Dry Texturizing Spray, for a subtly messy, matte look.” The makeup artist Gregory Arlt paired hair and clothes with M.A.C. products that conveyed, “Healthy tired. It might sound strange, but we imagined the guys looking warm and attractive, despite their penchant for partying.” Using just moisturizer (as opposed to foundation) for a base, Arlt slathered onto the models’ faces a yet to be released product from M.A.C.- Mineralize Charged Water Moisture Gel (hitting shelves this December). Brows were then defined and filled in with Kid eyeshadow, while lips were smoothed with lip conditioner. Lastly, he dotted on Select Moisturecover Concealer as necessary, so models looked “handsome, even after that long night out.”

headline.main: Runway Grooming Report | Antonio Azzuolo

docs.abstract: Like the look at Helmut Lang earlier today, the mandate is “wet,” but Alexander Wang-style.
docs.snippet: Like the look at Helmut Lang earlier today, the mandate is “wet,” but Alexander Wang-style.
docs.lead_paragraph: Backstage at Alexander Wang, 3:30 pm: Liya Kebede, in black jeans and Doc Martens, is having her hair examined by Guido Palau’s team. Nearby, Frankie Rayder is pulling on a black and red plaid lumberjack shirt over the plastic-bag poncho she’s wearing around her neck. It’s a makeshift protective cover for hair damp with product and oil. Like the look at Helmut Lang earlier today, the mandate is “wet,” but Alexander Wang-style, which translates into Palau using Redken’s Full Frame 07 All Over Volume Mousse to coat the head and then finishing off with Argan-6 oil right before the girls go out. “To get a glint in the hair,” is how Mr. Palau explained the addition of the multipurpose product. He is also adding extensions where needed and uses his Sultra curling iron for a little movement. With prints hitting the collection this season, Mr. Palau wanted to be sure the hair was edgy. “Pulled back can look too pretty,” he said, explaining the switch from last season’s low ponytail. “Today she’s let her hair down.” Both Mr. Palau and Diane Kendal agree that Mr. Wang has a very specific vision for his woman. She’s cool, downtown, beautiful and raw, as Ms. Kendal sees it. For makeup, this means M.A.C.’s black kohl pencil blended out around the eye and then removed with M.A.C. studio moisturizer and a cotton swab, only to be reapplied thereafter. There’s nothing on the face or lip. Nails are painted with Sally Hansen’s natural Parchment. Ms. Kendal has done this look before circa 1990. “Calvin went there,” she said before also calling out Helmut Lang. No doubt Mr. Wang remembers this girl and is now making her his own.

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Alexander Wang

docs.abstract: Despite the botched planning, the delays and bureaucratic politics, one official says, things are actually coming along very well in the World Trade Center area.
docs.snippet: Despite the botched planning, the delays and bureaucratic politics, one official says, things are actually coming along very well in the World Trade Center area.
docs.lead_paragraph: A DECADE after the Sept. 11 attack, downtown Manhattan is resurgent. The residential population has doubled. Two skyscrapers — 1 and 4 World Trade Center — are rising at ground zero, due to open in 2013. The next year, the exuberant PATH transit hub is scheduled to come online. The national memorial is open; two streets have been built. A far more diverse array of businesses call downtown home today, including a large cluster of media companies, law firms and nonprofit organizations. And just last week, both the northbound and southbound platforms of the Cortlandt Street subway station were open.

headline.main: Downtown’s Rebirth, 10 Years and $24 Billion Later

docs.lead_paragraph: North American moviegoers, jumping at the chance to see Gwyneth Paltrow and a host of other stars die of a horrible disease, drove “Contagion” to No. 1 at the weekend box office with an estimated $23 million in ticket sales. That Warner Brothers film, directed by Steven Soderbergh and made in conjunction with Participant Media, cost about $60 million to produce; an all-star cast (Kate Winslet, Matt Damon, Laurence Fishburne and Jude Law in addition to Ms. Paltrow) and strong reviews contributed to audience interest. “The Help” (DreamWorks Studios) was second, taking in about $8.7 million for a five-week total of $137 million, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles box-office statistics. “Warrior,” a mixed martial arts drama from Lionsgate, was a disappointing third with about $5.6 million in ticket sales. “The Debt” (Focus Features) took in roughly $5 million for fourth place, lifting its two-week total to $22 million. “Colombiana” (Sony Pictures Entertainment) was fifth with about $4 million in ticket sales and a new three-week total of $29.8 million. On the gloomy side, “Bucky Larson: Born to be a Star,” a Sony comedy produced by Adam Sandler’s company, took in just $1.5 million and placed far outside the top 10.

headline.main: ‘Contagion’ Is No. 1 at Weekend Box Office

HBO also received awards for the mini-series “Mildred Pierce,” a Lady Gaga tour special and a children’s program called “A Child’s Garden of Poetry.” The annual creative arts ceremony also recognized Justin Timberlake twice — once for guest-hosting “Saturday Night Live” and once for co-writing the lyrics to his “SNL” monologue song. Other stars who were recognized on Saturday include Gwyneth Paltrow, for her guest-star turn on “Glee”; Jay Leno, for his car Web site JayLenosGarage.com; and Jeff Probst, for his hosting of “Survivor.” The ceremony will be shown on the ReelzChannel on Saturday, a day before the prime-time awards are shown live on Fox.

docs.lead_paragraph: It’s not every morning that starts with someone referencing Catherine Deneuve and drugstores in the same sentence. It happened backstage at Victoria Beckham where Guido Palau explained that he was using “quite a lot of product” and Goody hair barrettes to channel Deneuve-like elegance with a masculine bent. This meant Redken Thickening Lotion spread throughout the hair for texture, with Hardwear at the center to make a wet-looking panel at the crown, which was pulled back with a classic silver clip (here’s where we get drugstore). Then loads of Hairspray 23 on the loose hair, “for texture, not hold,” Palau said. “Wet and dry, shine and matte,” is how he described the contrasts within the style. As the girls walked out, Palau added a little Glass Panel to heighten this effect.

docs.lead_paragraph: In both of the books she has written about American presidents, Candice Millard has zeroed in on events that other historians largely overlook. Her first book, “The River of Doubt,” followed Theodore Roosevelt’s strenuous efforts to regain his confidence after his failed 1912 third-party bid for re-election and described his near-disastrous journey down the Amazon tributary of the title. The details of this trip were hardly unknown, but they were easily overshadowed by other aspects of Roosevelt’s hugely eventful life. Ms. Millard turned a relative footnote into a newly mesmerizing story.

docs.snippet: “The White Box Project,” at the Black & White Gallery in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, blurs the line between audience and performers.
docs.lead_paragraph: Noémie Lafrance is a site-specific choreographer, which means that in her works, place is paramount. She’s staged dances in a 50,000-square-foot drained swimming pool and on the swooping rooftop of a Frank Gehry building. Her new installation, “The White Box Project,” is set at the Black & White Gallery in Williamsburg, Brooklyn — or, rather, behind it. A door at the back of the gallery opens onto a concrete courtyard, enclosed by whitish brick walls and exposed to the sky. It’s like a handball court that’s seen better days, a space small enough that when the cast of 20 dancers start running, everyone else better get out of the way. Unfortunately Ms. Lafrance’s guiding idea is even smaller.

It’s all about communication, people.

Still, Dimple, the London-raised daughter of a diplomat, barely resembles the demure Hindi-film heroines of yore. She knows what she wants, likes to have fun and enjoys being a bad girl. She even stages an unauthorized rock concert at the Agra fort, where — with the Taj Mahal for a backdrop — she wails on a shiny electric guitar in ripped pink jeans. docs.abstract: One woman’s violent wartime life along the Kentucky-Tennessee border.
docs.snippet: One woman’s violent wartime life along the Kentucky-Tennessee border.
docs.lead_paragraph: At around two in the morning on Sept. 7, 1861, Confederate soldiers burst into the home of Julia Marcum, intent on killing her father. They “broke the door open with bayonets on their guns and said there was 36 men around who had come to kill” him, she later wrote. The 16-year-old girl lived with her parents and five siblings on a farm in Scott County, Tenn., northwest of Knoxville near the Kentucky border. Like most of their neighbors, the Marcums were strong Unionists. Early in the war Julia’s father, Hiram, made his farm available as a way station for the thousands of Southern men traveling north to join Lincoln’s army, guiding many of them to the border himself.

headline.main: Julia Marcum’s Civil War

docs.snippet: Snyder was very eager to talk about the initiative he’d embarked upon to install solar panels atop FedEx field. He seemed less eager to discuss the general antipathy that has greeted his ownership from the media, fans and even a beloved Redskins H...
docs.lead_paragraph: Here are a few extras from my interview with the billionaire owner of the Washington Redskins, Daniel Snyder. We spoke on the afternoon of Aug. 22, just after he came off the field from watching his team practice at their Ashburn, Va., headquarters. Snyder was very eager to talk about the initiative he’d embarked upon to install solar panels atop FedEx field. He sent assistants scurrying about to bring in renderings of what the field will look like after NRG, the energy company, installs them. (NRG gets some very prominent signage at FedEx  for its efforts.) He seemed less eager to discuss the general antipathy that has greeted his ownership from the media, fans and even a beloved Redskins Hall of Fame Running back. Throughout the interview, he kept glancing uncomfortably at Tony Wyllie, the Redskins’ head of communications, who was sitting in. I honestly couldn’t tell whether he was shocked that I was pursuing that particular line of questioning, or if he was so insulated that he didn’t understand the depth and breadth of the criticism of the decisions he’s made as owner.

headline.main: Daniel Snyder, Owner of the Redskins, Keeps on Talking

docs.abstract: Arvo Pärt and the Norwegian architecture firm Snohetta collaborate with the Guggenheim Museum to quietly celebrate the city a decade after 9/11.
docs.snippet: Arvo Pärt and the Norwegian architecture firm Snohetta collaborate with the Guggenheim Museum to quietly celebrate the city a decade after 9/11.
docs.lead_paragraph: Sometimes all a New Yorker wants is a little peace and quiet. And on the extended weekends of Sept. 15-18 and Sept. 22-25, it will be available, in a very carefully fashioned version, at various locations around Lower Manhattan, as part of “To a Great City,” the second installment of “Stillspotting Nyc,” a two-year multidisciplinary program by the Guggenheim Museum. Organized by David van der Leer, the museum’s associate curator in architecture and urban studies, and Sarah Malaika, a project associate, “To a Great City” is a collaboration between the Estonian composer Arvo Part and the Norwegian architecture firm Snohetta. It creates urban soundscapes in five downtown locations that, according to the museum’s press release, “quietly celebrate the city, 10 years after the Sept. 11 attacks.” The locations include a green labyrinth created by the Battery Conservancy, an underground chamber at the Governors Island National Monument, and spaces in landmark skyscrapers that are normally inaccessible to the public. For a $10 admission fee, visitors will be given a map, directions and a one-day pass to each of the “stillspots” for a self-guided tour, which takes about three hours; reservations are recommended. In conjunction with the project, visitors can identify and map their own favorite quiet spots as part of “Create Your Own Stillspot” at stillspotting.guggenheim.org.

headline.main: Now Listening | Stillspotting

docs.abstract: Orlando Pita and James Kaliardos created a beehive hairdo and an earthy palette for Diane von Furstenberg’s collection.
docs.snippet: Orlando Pita and James Kaliardos created a beehive hairdo and an earthy palette for Diane von Furstenberg’s collection.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Am I done?” Joan Smalls asked Orlando Pita backstage at Diane von Furstenberg as he fixed her teased out beehive. “Done,” he said as she coyly examined his curly hair. “Done done?” Smalls asked knowing there may be yet another round of Orlando Pita hair spray to keep the look in place. Surprisingly, it wasn’t the ’60s that inspired the up-do that Pita referred to as “Kim Novak-y,” rather Von Furstenberg’s starting point for the collection: “New Beginnings.” For makeup, this meant James Kaliardos used M.A.C. products for a face inspired by the land where it all began: Africa. The idea was to highlight the planes and tones of the face using an earthy (literally) palette of eight Crème Color Base shades, including Ochre, Pale Peach and Dark Brown. The inner and outer corner of the eye was highlighted with a khaki variation, while the middle of the lid was done in white or yellow. There was no lip, just as nails were kept clean, coated with only Sally Hansen’s Hard as Nails. Kaliardos described the ingenuity of the woman who inspired him, “No matter her economic situation, she finds a way to look beautiful— regal even.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Diane von Furstenberg

On Monday, production began on “Quartet,” Mr. Hoffman’s feature-directing debut, its press representatives announced. The film, which is expected to shoot for nine weeks in Buckinghamshire, England, stars Tom Courtenay (whose previous films include “Doctor Zhivago” in 1965), Billy Connolly (“Mrs. Brown”) and Pauline Collins (“Shirley Valentine”) as residents of a home for retired opera singers. Their annual plans for a fund-raising concert, held on Verdi’s birthday, are disrupted by the arrival of a down-on-her-luck grande dame (played by Maggie Smith, the “Downton Abbey,” “Gosford Park” and “Harry Potter” star). The screenplay for “Quartet” is by Ronald Harwood, the Academy Award-winning screenwriter of “The Pianist” and “The Diving Bell and the Butterfly,” and adapted from his play of the same title. Mr. Hoffman is also a producer on the film, which is financed by BBC Films, DCM Productions and Decca. An American distributor and release date for “Quartet” were not immediately announced.

headline.main: Dustin Hoffman Graduates to Film Director

docs.lead_paragraph: It was the architect Richard Neutra’s rigorous West Coast houses that inspired the beauty look at Derek Lam — that and the color yellow. Both may be odd inspirations for hair and makeup, but that’s what makes them so welcome. Better yellow and geometry than another repeat reference, though the look wasn’t totally different from last time around. “This collection’s an evolution from last season, not a complete change,” Orlando Pita said. “The hair has that feeling too.” This meant a low side-parted ponytail instead of hair pulled back at the crown without a visible barrette. “Clean, simple lines,” is how Pita described the look he created using Phyto Volume Active Mousse, blow drying with a T3 featherweight Luxe, then sealing the ends with Phyto 7 and a T3 Single Pass iron. The hair was then scraped back into a ponytail with a part over the right eye. Pita used Phyto Finishing Spray and a little Shine Defining Wax to ”make it perfectly done.” Nails were painted Estée Lauder’s Nude Attitude, but it was the eyes that went a little wild. Tom Pecheux (Estée Lauder’s creative makeup director) explained the Neutra connection by making references to large windows that “let the outdoor weather into the house,” which became a ray of yellow from Estée Lauder Rain Boots shadow on the lid highlighted with Cyber Copper brown shimmer all the way to the brow bone. Citron Kiss lip gloss was the final step. Canary colored in the vial, it’s the perfect way to warm up another lip color or let the light in for spring.

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Derek Lam

docs.lead_paragraph: What makes a child nap? Most parents cherish toddlers’ naps as moments of respite and recharging, for parent and child alike; we are all familiar with the increased crankiness that comes when a nap is unduly delayed or evaded. docs.abstract: A move increased the term of copyright on sound recordings to 70 years from 50, while excluding any provision that would allow artists in Europe to recoup ownership of their music.
docs.snippet: A move increased the term of copyright on sound recordings to 70 years from 50, while excluding any provision that would allow artists in Europe to recoup ownership of their music.
docs.lead_paragraph: In a victory for the financially troubled recording industry, the European Union on Monday extended the term of copyright on sound recordings to 70 years from 50, while declining to include provisions that would allow artists in Britain and elsewhere in Europe to recoup ownership of their music easily. Had the Council of the European Union not acted, many of the most famous and popular recordings of the British Invasion of the 1960s, including albums by the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, the Who and the Yardbirds, would have fallen into the public domain in the coming years. For example, the Beatles’ first hit record, “Love Me Do,” which was released in 1962, could have been treated next year in much the same way as works by classical composers whose exclusive ownership of their music has expired. With multiple versions available at cheaper prices, the four major record labels would be deprived of one of their biggest sources of income.

headline.main: Europe Extends Copyright on Music
headline.print_headline: Europe Extends Copyright On Music

docs.abstract: Sleek and simple was the theme for hair and makeup at Tommy Hilfiger.
docs.snippet: Sleek and simple was the theme for hair and makeup at Tommy Hilfiger.
docs.lead_paragraph: “I’m not reinventing the wheel,” was how Eugene Souleiman introduced the sleek, simple ponytail at Tommy Hilfiger, before adding, “But for Tommy, I am. Because Tommy does that healthy, American girl with bouncy hair, and I’m doing something very clean, very sharp, and very chic.” This shift from previous seasons (it was Souleiman who was behind those healthy, bouncy heads of hair at the fall 2011 show) was implemented through flat ironing strands with the help of Wella’s Shine Finish, which he called “liquid gold,” then tucking hair back behind the ears before pulling it into a low ponytail tied with a thin black elastic. To achieve a graphic but not hard, product-y look, Souleiman squirted a bit of Wella Professionals Stay Essential Finishing Spray on a brush blush before running it over the surface of the hair to smooth down flyaways. As it turns out, it takes almost as much work to not reinvent the wheel as it does to invent it; as he noted, “It’s so easy to do something really wacky — I could do that with my eyes shut. But to think of something that has a subtlety and beauty to it, it’s so much harder.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Tommy Hilfiger

docs.abstract: A set of questions and puzzles exploring some of the truths and myths of the Golden Ratio and the Fibonacci sequence.
docs.snippet: A set of questions and puzzles exploring some of the truths and myths of the Golden Ratio and the Fibonacci sequence.
docs.lead_paragraph: Last week I attended a wonderful presentation given by Keith Devlin, a Stanford University mathematician and NPR’s “Math Guy,” on “Fibonacci & the Golden Ratio: Exposed Common Myths and Fascinating Truths” as part of the public lecture series “Math Encounters” organized by the Museum of Mathematics. The golden ratio or phi (1.61803…) is a fascinating number that we have explored before in the puzzles, Moonlighting Triangles and The Golden Ratio Treasure. The ratio, which is approached to greater and greater precision by two adjacent numbers of the related Fibonacci sequence (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13…), has become part of popular culture, attaining almost mystical status. Images and video clips like the one above abound on the Internet, connecting the golden ratio and the Fibonacci sequence with art, architecture, cosmology, biology, aesthetics, poetry, music and many other fields. But how much of all this is true and how much is myth? Professor Devlin, who recently published a scholarly book titled The Man of Numbers: Fibonacci’s Arithmetic Revolution, examined the evidence with a scientific eye and separated the wheat from the chaff. I present some of his findings below – in the form of questions to you, of course.

headline.main: Numberplay: Phi – The Magic and the Myth

docs.abstract: The Seattle City Council voted Monday to require employers with five or more workers to provide paid sick days.
docs.snippet: The Seattle City Council voted Monday to require employers with five or more workers to provide paid sick days.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Seattle City Council voted Monday to require employers with five or more workers to provide paid sick days. Supporters said they expected Mayor Mike McGinn to approve the legislation, which would make Seattle one of three major cities, along with San Francisco and Washington, to require paid sick days. Connecticut is the only state to enact paid sick days for private employers. The Seattle vote was 8 to 1, with the City Council president, Richard Conlin, opposing. Companies with 5 to 49 workers would have to offer full-time workers at least five paid sick days yearly, while the largest companies would have to provide at least nine. Supporters said it was important for public health that food-service and health-care workers have paid sick days, but business opponents said the legislation was an expensive mandate.

headline.main: Seattle Council Votes for Paid Sick Time

docs.abstract: Of maps and territories.
docs.snippet: Of maps and territories.
docs.lead_paragraph: Mark Thoma objects to Tyler Cowen’s attempt to pigeonhole some of us as “Old New Keynesians”, and makes the case for flexibility in use of models. Indeed. But there’s something more systematic to the macro story – something that very much informs my work. Namely, “old Keynesian” and “new Keynesian” models represent two intelligent but imperfect responses to the problem of thinking about an economy in which people must make future-oriented decisions. Neither is fully convincing, but there are no better alternatives at this point. So what I do, and I hope others do as well, is to think about policy issues both ways, and try to “bracket” things in a way that leads to reasonably secure conclusions.

headline.main: How Much Hoc to Add? (Wonkish and Methodological)

docs.abstract: Guido Palau and Dick Page discuss the hair and makeup for the Spring 2012 show.
docs.snippet: Guido Palau and Dick Page discuss the hair and makeup for the Spring 2012 show.
docs.lead_paragraph: You know you’re a beauty industry rock star when a designer makes references to your past work in his preshow brief. “Nineties Guido,” was what Marc Jacobs wanted for Marc by Marc Jacobs according to Guido Palau backstage before the show. “They got out all my old pictures,” he said of the stack of images unearthed by Jacobs’s team. In the end, Palau came up with a half pulled-through ponytail created by first blow-drying the hair with Redken Satinwear, then pulling it back with an elastic. The next step was attaching the tail to the back of the head with a silver Goody clip and coating the hair with Shine Enrich and Forceful 23 Spray. “A little bit spiky — aerodynamic,” is how Palau described the finished look. Nails were painted Zoya’s Olivia with a custom matte top coat to make a nude velvet effect. For makeup, Dick Page conceived what he referred to as the appropriately collegiate “Pretty 101, just a healthy face.” This was done using Shiseido gold blush dusted just above the cheek bones with a rosy tone below. Eyelids were spread with Shiseido Maquillage Lip Gloss and brows were colored with Shimmering Cream eyeshadow in one of four shades: Sable, Gold Meadow, Caviar or Leather, a reddish brown for those with auburn hair. Roseate was dabbed onto the bare mouth with the finger. Said Page, “Nothing too complicated, no tricks.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Marc by Marc Jacobs

docs.abstract: James Kaliardos and Odile Gilbert discuss hair and makeup for the Spring 2012 collection.
docs.snippet: James Kaliardos and Odile Gilbert discuss hair and makeup for the Spring 2012 collection.
docs.lead_paragraph: Backstage at Rodarte, James Kaliardos was touching up Kate Mulleavy’s makeup while one of his assistants prepped the model Samantha Gradoville (wearing her own webby, iridescent knit) nearby. Odile Gilbert was on the other side of the space getting girls ready for what she calls the “Sweet 16,” an off-center part with a natural wave and one side twisted up and tucked in with a comb. “Soft, innocent — not pretentious,” she said of the style created with Kérastase Volume Active Mousse and Double Force hairspray. “It looks easy, but it’s not easy.” Deborah Lippman painted toes Fashion, her opaque beige, and fingers a custom variation of Lady Sings the Blues. The Mulleavy sisters asked her to up the amount of large graphite glitter in the polish rather than the standard mix of paillettes. Like Lippman, Kaliardos channeled Van Gogh’s “Starry Night” with dark navy, shimmering eyes. Using Nars products, he drew all over lids with the shadow pencil in Dark Night and then added Night Flight and Tropic, a turquoise glitter. “Looks a bit like Edvard Munch’s ‘The Scream,'” Kaliardos said laughing as he moved on from Van Gogh. Penny Lane cream blush was used high on the cheeks and to cover the lips, which were then coated with Pearl Beach eyeshadow and Na Na gloss. “Dreamy and aggressive at the same time,” he said. “A cool, ethereal girl.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Rodarte

docs.lead_paragraph: Some designers this week released their inner gypsies, unveiling collections that brimmed with violently colorful, multicultural references. Some shows carried a whiff of Haiti or Hawaii, while others mined the landscapes and cultures of India and North Africa. Embracing a vagabond spirit,Thakoon Panichgul married the exoticism of Bollywood with broad hints of the American West; Donna Karan combined Haitian-inspired geometry with a dusky African palette, Duro Olowu offered an homage to his Jamaican-born mum, and Joseph Altuzarra showed a smattering of hothouse florals redolent of the South Pacific. It’s a global marketplace, they say, in more ways than one.

docs.lead_paragraph: Lt. Col. Charles de Choiseul was not a happy man. It was September 1861, and de Choiseul, a well-educated French Creole, had been ordered to take temporary command of Maj. Chatham Roberdeau Wheat’s First Special Battalion of Louisiana Infantry while Wheat recovered from a serious wound suffered at the First Battle of Bull Run. It was no routine assignment: a Virginia officer had been given the position previously, but he was unable to control the rowdy men and quit after only a few days. Now it was de Choiseul’s turn to try to rein in what was known as the Tiger Battalion. He wrote a friend, “I am a victim of circumstances, not of my own will. … Whether the Tigers will devour me, or whether I will succeed in taming them, remains to be seen.”

headline.main: The Terrifying Tigers

Any one race may or may not be representative.

docs.lead_paragraph: Finally, something for the J. K. Rowling fan who has everything, including some extra space in his or her shoe closet. Arriving on the heels, so to speak, of Tuesday’s announcement that a one-sentence letter from J. D. Salinger to his maid was being offered for $50,000, a company in Omaha is putting up for auction a pair of boots that Ms. Rowling wore while she wrote the first book in her best-selling “Harry Potter” series. The boots, which are being sold by Blue Earth Benefit Auctions in an online auction that starts Friday at proxibid.com, were given to a fifth-grade class at Harrison Elementary School in Omaha in 1999. At that time, the class was conducting a project called “Operation Shoe Tree,” in which celebrities or other people the pupils admired were asked to write about their lives from the perspective of their footwear.

docs.abstract: A design and architecture movement is sweeping through Istanbul.
docs.snippet: A design and architecture movement is sweeping through Istanbul.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Design is not about objects anymore; it’s more pervasive,” says Vasif Kortun, a director of Istanbul’s new arts center Salt (Istiklal Caddesi 136; saltonline.org). “Turkey is picking it up belatedly.” And quickly. Since the opening of Adnan Kazmaoglu’s austerely geometric Yesil Vadi Mosque in Istanbul last year, a design and architecture movement is sweeping through the city. Salt’s Beyoglu building, a columned space by the local architect Han Tumertekin on the boulevard Istiklal, features the work of a different Turkish designer in each room — there’s a cinema by Hakan Demirel, a bookstore by Omer Unal and a cafe by Ali Selcuk and the chef Murat Bozok. Regular symposiums cover everything from urban planning to electronic music, and later this fall a second outpost will open nearby in Galata.

docs.abstract: Orlando Pita and Dick Page on the hair and makeup for Kors’s Spring 2012 collection.
docs.snippet: Orlando Pita and Dick Page on the hair and makeup for Kors’s Spring 2012 collection.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Michael loves a bronze girl or boy,” said Dick Page backstage at Michael Kors. “This is a sort of rough glamor.” Page used Shiseido Creme Shadow in Caviar, Leather and Sable to create strong eyebrows with Meadow gold spread on the lid and Caramel Perfect Rouge on the lips. Luminize Satin Face Color in BE 206 was mixed with Bronzer 1 and 2 all over the face to make sure the models “didn’t look like they had to get up at 6 a.m. to do a show.” No one did. “It’s pretty,” Hanne Gaby said of her tousled hair braided with black leather. “I don’t think I’d be able to do it, though.” Luckily, Orlando Pita was there to help create the look that came about based on one of Kors’s fantasy stories. (“He embellished it more than I do,” said Pita of the designer’s storytelling prowess.) The tales goes: These girls are on a trip in Africa with only shoelaces to tie back their hair. “They groom themselves,” said Pita. “The front is all they can see.” This explains why the hair around the face was more tidy, parted in the middle, while the back was wild and messy. Orlando’s own Dry Shampoo was used with Bumble and Bumble Surf Spray to coat the hair before braiding. The tail was then teased up between the lacing and Pita’s Elevate Texture Spray added. The model Magdalena Frackowiak offered a way to translate the look to her own routine: “braid it loosely and then pull bits out.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Michael Kors

docs.lead_paragraph: No act in contemporary pop is more careful than the bionic country trio Lady Antebellum, which never leaves a note out of place, which never lets a feeling spill outside the lines. It takes basic components — male-female harmony, sturdy pop arrangements with light brushes of country, an unerring sense of when to shift a song from desperate to redemptive — and arranges them in several different ways, with mostly similar results. These are plain and obvious tricks, shopworn from years of deployment. Lady Antebellum songs don’t try to hide anything. It’s infuriating.

docs.abstract: J. Crew’s first ever presentation for New York fashion week featured clever, impeccably styled pieces in bright colors, plaids and polka dots.
docs.snippet: J. Crew’s first ever presentation for New York fashion week featured clever, impeccably styled pieces in bright colors, plaids and polka dots.
docs.lead_paragraph: J. Crew staged its highly anticipated, first-ever New York Fashion Week presentation at the tents in Lincoln Center this season. The men’s collection, designed by Frank Muytjens, included some greatest hits of American sportswear (the perfect slender suits and sports jackets, sailor-striped knits and tailored trousers) alongside clever pieces in bright colors, plaids and polka dots, always impeccably styled. The cuffed khakis lined with St. James stripes were absolutely charming, but my favorite look was on the more minimal side. A stone-colored jean jacket, buttoned all the way up and worn with matching jean-style trousers, topped by a navy nylon lightweight parka, was the winner for me. docs.snippet: In a statement on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Society of St. Pius X must accept the terms of a “doctrinal preamble,” before a “hoped for reconciliation” could be reached.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Vatican on Wednesday told a breakaway traditionalist group with which Pope Benedict XVI has taken pains to reconcile that it must accept certain church teachings before being fully brought back into the Roman Catholic Church. The Vatican’s chief doctrinal officer, Cardinal William J. Levada, met with Bishop Bernard Fellay of the Society of St. Pius X, which split with Rome to protest the liberalizing reforms of the Second Vatican Council. In 1988, Pope John Paul II excommunicated the group's founder, Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, as well as four bishops he consecrated without the approval of the Vatican, including Bishop Fellay. In 2009, Benedict lifted the excommunications of the four bishops, even though one of them, Richard Williamson, had denied the scope of the Holocaust.

headline.main: Vatican Gives Group Reconciliation Path

docs.lead_paragraph: There are three ways to make the recipe that follows here; three pathways to dinnertime nirvana. The dish is the Korean barbecue standard known as bulgogi — “fire meat,” is the literal translation — transformed into a sandwich filling, a sloppy Joe for a more perfect union. (File under “Blessings of Liberty.”) Fed to children with a tall glass of milk, the sandwiches may inspire smiles and licked plates, rapt attention and the request that the meal be served at least monthly — they are not at all too spicy for younger palates. Given to adults accompanied by cold lager, cucumber kimchi and a pot of the fermented Korean hot-pepper paste known as gochujang, they can rise to higher planes.

docs.lead_paragraph: The phone rang, and my stomach clenched when I heard her voice. “Daddy? I want to go home,” said my 8-year-old daughter, Arden. Two hours earlier, I dropped Arden and her two siblings off at their new school in a squat building in a forest of Soviet-era apartment blocks on Krasnoarmeyskaya (Red Army) Street in Moscow. Mr. Polanski, the director of films including “Rosemary’s Baby,” “Chinatown” and “The Pianist” was arrested at the request of the United States when he arrived in 2009 at the Zurich airport en route to the festival. Prosecutors in Los Angeles and Washington were seeking to extradite the filmmaker, who fled the United States in 1978 to avoid facing punishment after he pleaded guilty one year earlier to having sex with a 13-year-old girl. Mr. Polanski spent several months under house arrest in Gstaad before Swiss prosecutors said they would not extradite him.

docs.snippet: The barrier for entry into the jock memoir genre is, unsurprisingly, pretty low. For every “Open” — Andre Agassi’s much-acclaimed, lovely autobiography — there are a dozen or so books like “Outrageous!,” the decidedly less literary reminiscences o...
docs.lead_paragraph: The barrier for entry into the jock memoir genre is, unsurprisingly, pretty low. For every “Open” — Andre Agassi’s much-acclaimed, lovely autobiography — there are a dozen or so books like “Outrageous!,” the decidedly less literary reminiscences of Charles Barkley, in which the author famously claimed he was misquoted. Sure, ghostwriters have something to do with this, but at least “Outrageous!” was about Charles Barkley — a controversial N.B.A. Hall of Famer who played with and against some of the league’s all-time greats. What has always confounded me is the sheer number of ordinary, even journeyman athletes who cash in by documenting their rise to midlevel greatness between hard covers. But since so many of them do it, here are my favorites. (Intentionally missing is Jim Bouton’s totally awesome, gossip-laden “Ball Four.” Though Bouton was the definition of a mediocre player, he remains the Homer of the genre he created. Simply put, it’s not fair to compare him to anyone.)

headline.main: My Three Favorite Journeyman-Athlete Memoirs

docs.abstract: The Los Angeles artist Bettina Hubby, true to her name, is fascinated with the institution of matrimony.
docs.snippet: The Los Angeles artist Bettina Hubby, true to her name, is fascinated with the institution of matrimony.
docs.lead_paragraph: Her last name means partner or husband, and her parents have married and divorced each other more than once. So it’s no surprise that the Los Angeles artist Bettina Hubby is fascinated with the institution of matrimony. “Marriage is a big topic for me,” she said. “I was married and so were my parents, several times, and I wondered why marriage hasn’t changed or evolved the way other things have changed.” In 2009 she initiated Get Hubbied, a multitiered art project to investigate the idea of marriage, which she describes as both fragile and resilient. Hubby and the artist and musician Tif Sigfrids, who have been working together for the last four years, conducted intensive research into all aspects of marriage and the rituals surrounding the wedding ceremony.

headline.main: Seeing Things | Getting Hubbied

docs.abstract: Odile Gilbert and Francelle Daly discuss the hair and makeup for the Spring 2012 collection.
docs.snippet: Odile Gilbert and Francelle Daly discuss the hair and makeup for the Spring 2012 collection.
docs.lead_paragraph: On what’s supposed to be the last day of summer weather, a cool breeze was appropriately the inspiration for Odile Gilbert’s hair backstage at Phillip Lim. After coating strands with Kérastase Fibre Architecte, a yet to be released product that’s both a texturizer and a treatment conditioner, she parted straightened hair on the side and separated it into two low ponytails. These were then knotted at the neck and four little strands were pinned to the head as if blown back by a gust of wind. Perhaps in an allusion to the raincoats in the collection, nails were painted a custom blend of CND Raspberry Parfait, Guava and Speedy top coat. Francelle Daly for Nars created what she described as “dewy, fresh, skin” with Radiant Tinted Moisturizer intended to contrast “a edgy, heavy metallic eye.” Night Life shadow was applied in the crease to make a demi lune; underneath it, a hollow of bare skin. The silver Paris Duo was used along the eyebrow and Rue Bonaparte neutral liner in the duct. Not one but six coats of mascara were applied to lashes. “Romantic and rebel,” is how Daly explained this juxtaposition. Lips were covered in concealer and topped with Gaiete blush to create color in a fresh way. You know, these things change with the wind.

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Phillip Lim

docs.lead_paragraph: President Obama is awarding Marine Cpl. Dakota Meyer the U.S. Medal of Honor for his valor during a 2009 battle in Afghanistan’s Kunar Province. Corporal Meyer, 23, is credited with saving the lives of 36 Marines and soldiers — 13 Americans and 23 Afghans, when he charged repeatedly into a Taliban-held area after learning that four American military personnel — three fellow Marines and a Navy corpsman — were missing. Corporal Meyer came under heavy fire, but located and retrieved his fallen comrades from the battlefield with the help of a Afghan troops. He is only the third living veteran to receive the award for service in Afghanistan or Iraq and the first living Marine to receive the award since 1973.

docs.abstract: With its rich cultural traditions and an architectural heritage that spans the centuries, Quito is more than just a stop on the way to the Galápagos.
docs.snippet: With its rich cultural traditions and an architectural heritage that spans the centuries, Quito is more than just a stop on the way to the Galápagos.
docs.lead_paragraph: NESTLED amid snowcapped Andean peaks, Ecuador’s capital has long been overlooked by travelers on their way to the country’s most famous destination, the Galápagos Islands. But visitors who bypass this lively historic city of some two million people are missing out. At 9,350 feet above sea level, on the eastern slopes of the Pichincha Volcano, Quito offers breathtaking vistas around nearly every corner. Its historic center, a Unesco World Heritage site, is one of the largest in South America, with 40 colonial churches and chapels, 16 convents and monasteries and picturesque plazas. In recent years, museums have been opened; mansions restored; hotels, restaurants and cafes opened and safety improved. And this year, in recognition of Quito’s rich mix of architectural heritage and cultural traditions, the International Cultural Capitals Bureau chose the city as its 2011 American Capital of Culture.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Quito, Ecuador

docs.snippet: “In the spring of 1990 I packed up as much of my life in London as would ﬁt into a suitcase and four large plywood boxes and ﬂew to Seattle to set up house.”
docs.lead_paragraph: In the spring of 1990 I packed up as much of my life in London as would ﬁt into a suitcase and four large plywood boxes and ﬂew to Seattle to set up house. It was a selﬁsh and irregular move. I had “met someone” and liked what I’d seen of the Paciﬁc Northwest during a two-month stay there the previous autumn. I liked the aquarium lighting, the sawtooth alps forested with black ﬁrs, the compact cities encrusted in dirty Roman esque stucco. Most of all, I liked the place’s wateriness. At forty-seven I felt cracked and dry. My new home territory was as rainy as Ireland, puddled with lakes and veined with big rivers. Seattle was built out on pilings over the sea, and at high tide the whole city seemed to come aﬂoat like a ship lifting free from a mud berth and swaying in its chains.

headline.main: ‘Driving Home’

The sides were then pressed down with fingers. Campbell finished styles by showering hair with Redken Shine Flash 02 Glistening Mist and Cutler Shine Tattoo for an extreme, wet-looking finish. The makeup artist Yadim kept things aglow by moisturizing with Sisleÿum Global Revitalizer for Men, then tapping Sisley Radiant Immediate Lift on the high planes of the face to highlight. Phyto-Ombre Eclat Eye Shadow in Quartz was smudged on upper and lower lash lines “to enhance tone, like the boys have been out all night.” Yadim said. And just minutes before the show, Yadim slicked Confort Creme Lip Balm on lips and eyelids to complete “a face that looks as it’s been flooded in light.”

docs.snippet: Leah Hager Cohen’s fourth novel weaves a complex pattern of light and dark, happiness and grief, in a 21st-century version of the family chronicle.
docs.lead_paragraph: Leah Hager Cohen is one of our foremost chroniclers of the mundane complexities, nuanced tragedies and unexpected tendernesses of human connection. She earned her reputation with heralded books of nonfiction like “Train Go Sorry” and the novel “House Lights.” Impressively, her fourth novel, “The Grief of Others,” is her best work yet. Six complex but fundamentally decent characters hurt one another and are hurt by forces greater than themselves, whether those forces be the impersonal cruelty of nature’s accidents or the very personal torments of marriage and middle school. The overarching question is whether the members of the Ryrie family will piece themselves together and re-find who they all were during a halcyon vacation eight years past, or whether they will let sorrow, secrets and shame drive them irreparably apart.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Straw Dogs” — Rod Lurie’s odd and interesting remake of Sam Peckinpah’s venerable and violent button pusher — begins with a clash of cultural stereotypes. David Sumner (James Marsden) is a Hollywood screenwriter with an Ivy League education (or at least a Harvard T-shirt and fond memories of the Harvard-Yale game), newly arrived in his wife’s hometown, Blackwater, Miss. He is an effete coastal liberal, the kind of person who orders light beer at the local bar and grill, disdains its celebrated fried pickles and tries to pay with a credit card. He listens to classical music, uses big words like “acutely” and stays in shape by jumping rope. He can’t fix a roof or change a tire.

docs.lead_paragraph: TORONTO — Having muscled its way forward with ambition and mountains of money, the Toronto International Film Festival stands supreme as the leading cinema event after Cannes. This year’s event was the first time that the Bell Lightbox, the festival’s permanent home here, was fully operational. For much of the festival’s 11 days (it ends on Sunday), the five public theaters of the Lightbox are a home away from home for locals and globe-trotting professionals who also make camp in adjacent theaters, including a 14-screen multiplex with its own Burger King. They do things big here: more than 300 movies on 33 screens for admissions that, last year, topped a quarter-million.

docs.lead_paragraph: WHAT may be the biggest architecture event of the year ahead has not yet been scheduled. But when it happens, it’ll be a doozy: MGM Resorts International recently announced its intention to demolish the Harmon, a tower by Norman Foster that is a prominent component of the new CityCenter development in Las Vegas. Construction flaws were found years ago, and the building was never completed or occupied. Still, the spectacle of a boom-time project by one of the world’s most celebrated designers razed by a controlled implosion is sure to spark talk about the state of architecture today.

docs.lead_paragraph: The curse of Carrie Bradshaw infects “I Don’t Know How She Does It” with a severe case of what might be called post-Carrie Parkeritis. Parkeritis, if you haven’t heard, is the term given to a new ailment named after Sarah Jessica Parker, in which a star finds herself condemned to eke out the last drops of freshness from the role (in this case in “Sex and the City”) that made her world famous eons ago. In its chemical structure it closely resembles the Roberts Syndrome (as in Julia), first identified in “Pretty Woman” and last seen in “Larry Crowne.”

docs.lead_paragraph: The Iraqi president has been negotiating with Iranian officials in an attempt to gain the release of two American hikers held in Iran on espionage and trespassing convictions, according to Kurdish officials in Iraq. The president, Jalal Talabani, has been told by Iranian officials that the hikers will probably be released, the officials said. Iran’s president, Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, had said that the hikers, Shane M. Bauer and Joshua F. Fattal, would be freed by Thursday, but Iran’s judiciary ruled otherwise. The conflicting messages are believed to reflect a power struggle between Mr. Ahmadinejad and Iran’s conservative establishment. Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton said Thursday the United States had “received word through a number of sources” that the men would be released, despite the apparent confusion in Iran.

docs.lead_paragraph: In 1972, Massimo Vignelli designed a diagrammatic map for the New York City subway. It was a radical departure. He replaced the serpentine maze of geographically accurate train routes with simple, bold bands of color that turned at 45- and 90-degree angles. Each route was color-coded, its stops indicated by black dots. Its abstract representation of the routes was elegant but flawed. To make the map function effectively, a few geographic liberties were taken, something that didn’t sit well with New Yorkers.

docs.lead_paragraph: Eagles (1-0) at Falcons (0-1)Sunday, 8:20 p.m.Line: Eagles by 2 1/2In honor of Michael Vick’s return to Atlanta, the Eagles have starting using their 1989 throwback offense. The scheme pays homage to Randall Cunningham’s glory days. The Eagles do not really drive down the field; they just string together amazing highlights, interspersing the occasional punt or baffling mistake. A typical play begins with two defenders knifing untouched through Philadelphia’s porous, inexperienced offensive line. Vick either gets flattened or performs some Matrix-style escape, scrambling for a big gain or tossing to a receiver who used the confusion to get wide open. Andy Reid calls for a timeout four or five times per half to impose order (teams only get three timeouts per half, but a 5-yard penalty is a small price to pay for the chance to install a precisely designed sequence of plays for Vick to scrap).

docs.abstract: The Moscow’s Bolshoi Theater, after closing in 2005, will reopen next month with a gala performance of the ballet and opera companies’ greatest hits.
docs.snippet: The Moscow’s Bolshoi Theater, after closing in 2005, will reopen next month with a gala performance of the ballet and opera companies’ greatest hits.
docs.lead_paragraph: After closing its doors in 2005 for a rafters-to-orchestra-pit renovation, Moscow’s Bolshoi Theater still kicked up controversy — embezzlement, corruption, sex scandal. Now, three years past due and way over budget, the hall, which dates to 1825, will reopen next month with a gala performance of the ballet and opera companies’ greatest hits. In attendance will be President Dmitri Medvedev and other heads of state, who will finally see what $760 million restores. It took more than 3,500 workers to restore the Apollo and the Muses ceiling piece, replicate the missing Villeroy & Boch tiles and hang 617 pounds of crystal from the main chandelier. Much of the work was supervised by the president’s office itself, which stepped in when construction faltered in 2009, after a contractor was paid three times for the same work. Now the acoustics are fixed, subterranean hydraulic stages are built, and, for the finishing touch, the Romanov coat of arms has been reinstated above the lintels, in place of the hammer and sickle.

docs.abstract: “Rock ‘n’ roll on the Riviera” sums up beauty backstage at the L’Wren Scott show.
docs.snippet: “Rock ‘n’ roll on the Riviera” sums up beauty backstage at the L’Wren Scott show.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Rock ‘n’ roll on the Riviera” is the beauty catchphrase backstage at L’Wren Scott. “A contessa from wherever,” is how Serge Normant described the woman that inspired the undone French twists he created using his own line of products. He coated hair with Meta Lush Volumizer and Meta Revive Dry Shampoo before blow-drying and using a small barrel curling iron to create the base for finger waves. Then, the back was swept to the side and tucked into a twist secured with pins. “Sophistication becomes disheveled,” Normant said, using his fingers to pull apart the up do. Nails went the way of the lady, as well. “She wanted something sexy, nothing dark or overpowering of the clothes,” Yuna Park said of Blush, the custom mauve polish she created for Scott to replace last season’s black varnish. “It’s less Gothic, more feminine — not so harsh.” For makeup, Aaron De May translated Scott’s directive with a dense shiny eye, bronzed skin and a subtle lip. “Normally, L’Wren always likes strong, smoky, colorful, this was also about decadence, the duchesses, princesses arriving on boat in the ’40s and ’50s,” he said. De May used Lancôme Star Bronzer  in Solaire to make each girl’s skin color “two tones darker.” He then applied Le Crayon Kohl in Black Coffee all around the eye and in the crease. This was blended with Mochaccino shadow on the top and Vintage Brown on the bottom. He painted the inner corners of the eye gold from the 5 Pan Palette in Gold Frenzy and spread Juicy Tubes Pure clear lip gloss on the lid. “It can look dull or muddy with all that brown,” De May said. “This brings life to the face in need of a little bit of sparkle.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | L’Wren Scott

docs.lead_paragraph: I bought a house that a previous owner had nearly destroyed. He knocked holes in walls and doors, trucked away the deck and trashed the aboveground pool, etc. I assumed he was angry at his wife, but it turned out that he was angry at the bank, which had foreclosed, taking everything the couple had put into the property. When a mutual friend invited the former owners to visit, the wife wept and said she could never bear to see our improvements on a house that had been “stolen.” I know we didn’t steal her home, but I resolved never to buy a foreclosed house again. docs.lead_paragraph: “To start with, look at all the books.” That’s the promising first sentence of Jeffrey Eugenides’s new novel, “The Marriage Plot,” due in bookstores this fall. The book is about three college friends from Brown University, and at first taste — I’ve been toting around an advance copy — it appears to be luscious: humane, recondite and funny. Part of the heavy anticipation for “The Marriage Plot,” though, is a simple emotional response: We’ve missed this man. It has been nine years since Eugenides’s last novel, the Pulitzer Prize-winning “Middlesex.” It has been a long, lonely vigil. We’d nearly forgotten he was out there.

Depending on how you count, I may be twice as old as the traditional students or essentially the same age as they are. After all, my life as I know it began 23 years ago, when, in a freakish accident, I was hit in the head by a ceiling fan in our home in Fort Worth, Tex. docs.lead_paragraph: Jonathan Chait fundamentally misunderstands the left’s disapproval of President Obama. Yes, dissatisfaction with his handling of the stimulus and recession factors into it, but more important, the left finds him politically feckless and to have abandoned principles without having won political battles. His desire to create comity is admirable in theory, but compromise for its own sake is neither effective nor politically desirable. Perhaps we on the left misjudged Candidate Obama, but his campaign rhetoric was far more progressive than his presidency has been. We know he’s constrained by the Republican House, though there are areas in which he could achieve change, like closing Guantánamo, protecting whistle-blowers or, most important, withdrawing forces from Afghanistan. He could use ye olde Bully Pulpit to advocate progressive ideals vocally. That’s what “the left” wanted to see from Obama and why we are dissatisfied with him now.

docs.abstract: On one block in Brooklyn, food stamps and $185 meals are a contrast in economic extremes that may as well have come from the mind of a satirist.

docs.lead_paragraph: For decades, the intersection of Park Avenue and 96th Street has remained one of the city’s most obvious and despairing emblems of disparity, with East Harlem and its challenges spreading out to the north, and a vast gridlock of extraordinary privilege colonizing the acreage below. It is worth debating whether a visit to this corner ought to be mandated for tourists; few spots so profoundly render the truths of New York’s economic extremism. Liberal parents hoping to foster their own political values in their children might consider pilgrimages. When I stood there, as a teenager, for the first time in the early 1980s, I felt a call to fierce and equalizing justice, ready, suddenly, for Latin American guerrilla work and the Red Brigades.

docs.snippet: Jonathan Raban’s essays describe how he left England for a new life in Seattle.
docs.lead_paragraph: For the essayist the past is less a foreign country than a home address, a lodestar or touchstone, in Phillip Lopate's words the “Aladdin’s lamp which he or she never tires of rubbing.” It is more markedly so in a collection assembled over time, or in the case of Jonathan Raban, over the two decades this eloquent Englishman has spent in America. Raban presents his selections humbly, mindful of the gap that separates American from British English. “The longer I stay here,” he writes, “the more conscious I am of nuances to which I must still remain deaf.” It is impossible not to take to the author of a book called “Driving Home” who reveals that on his arrival he made the greatest of idiomatic American mistakes: he bought the wrong car. Less than gently, the woman for whom he had crossed the ocean translates. What message does his black Dodge Daytona communicate? “Midlife crisis,” she answers. “Who drives them?” he asks. “Kids. Black teenagers. Gang members,” she replies, crisply. She sounds very much aware that she is interpreting for a man who previously assumed Oregon to be an invention of Bernard Malamud.

docs.lead_paragraph: The unmarried black woman is a figure of cultural fascination these days. Cable news specials, popular books by Steve Harvey and T. D. Jakes, the films of Tyler Perry, and newspaper articles about single black women and their children born out of wedlock send waves of dismay through the American public. The explanations offered for this phenomenon tend to be of two sorts: prurient accounts of black male promiscuity and irresponsibility, or caricatures of aggressive and unreasonable black women. It is rare for the popular media to include careful social or historical analyses. Rather, they are often purveyors of a moral panic presented without root or reason.

docs.lead_paragraph: The project of the Indian republic has never been short on ambition. It now cinches 1.2 billion people into a pluralist democracy, and its recent experiments with economic reform have made the project still bolder. Perhaps this is why the moment seems to call for nonfiction about India that must match its subject for ambition. The platonic ideal of this book requires it to be rewarding to both Indians and outsiders; to possess the fluid art of literature but also the sweat-stained craft of journalism; to be encyclopedic and anecdotal; and to seek, within its characters, metaphors for their country at large.

docs.lead_paragraph: Hugh Thomas’s big new book falls firmly into the genre of Nobody Does This Anymore. “The Golden Empire” is the second installment in a multi­volume history of the rise of the Spanish Empire. The whole enterprise will surely comprise 2,000 pages or more; this present book clocks in at almost 700 pages, including five of intricate genealogical charts. The last historian of imperial Spain to work on this scale published his first volume in 1918, and the fourth and final volume didn’t appear for 26 years. Baron Thomas of Swynnerton, as Thomas is officially known, works much faster. If he keeps up the present rate of production, he might be able to lay down his pen after only 16.

docs.lead_paragraph: We might as well call it: The American left is dead. Faced with the greatest crisis of capitalism in almost a century, the left has mounted no effective mass protests, inspired no significant uprisings, spawned no major institutions or policy revolutions. In Wisconsin, labor unions lost their greatest public battle since Ronald Reagan’s showdown with air traffic controllers. In the midterm elections, the Tea Party, not the left, took advantage of economic discontent to upend the status quo. Today, the dream of socialism exists mostly as a far-right phantom, to be conjured up when Democrats dare to imply that Medicare or Social Security might serve the public good.

docs.lead_paragraph: Imani Perry, a distinguished scholar of law, literature, and American culture and history who is currently on the faculty of the Center for African American Studies at Princeton, this week reviews “Is Marriage for White People?” by the Stanford law professor Ralph Richard Banks. Combining academic research with personal interviews, Banks’s book investigates trends in marriage among African-Americans and asks how these may extend to society at large. Perry said via e-mail that she favors Banks’s approach: “It’s wonderful to match up human voices with more abstract analyses. I believe in employing many tools for pursuing an answer to a challenging problem. I’ll read poetry, neuroscience, psychology, media studies, and political, literary and social theory, all for a single project.”

docs.lead_paragraph: JAZZ pianists spend a lot of time alone with their craft, and often just as much in the context of a rhythm section. (It happened a lot in the 1930s among Harlem stride masters, behind closed doors, in clubby camaraderie.) The scarcity is enough to make you notice a good piano-duo album when it arrives. docs.lead_paragraph: LESSONS FROM TWAIN: Next month, the perennial best sellers David Baldacci, John Grisham and Jodi Picoult will appear together at Yale to discuss Mark Twain’s influence on their work. It’s not the most intuitive topic, as Picoult acknowledges: “Most of my Twain was read when I was a student, the same as most American kids,” she said by phone recently from her home in New Hampshire, “and I haven’t had the time to reread him since.” Yet Picoult — who spent nine weeks on the hard­cover fiction list this spring with “Sing You Home,” a novel about gay parenthood and embryonic rights — argues convincingly for Twain as a role model, emphasizing “how he balanced social commentary with a commercial fiction appeal.”

docs.lead_paragraph: “The New Teen Titans” omnibus, Vol. 1, sits atop the hardcover list this week. It reprints the first 16 issues of the 1980s series that brought together a few sidekick heroes (Robin, Kid Flash and Wonder Girl) and teamed them with some new ones (Cyborg, Raven and Starfire). These Titans, written by Marv Wolfman and illustrated by George Pérez, become one of DC’s most popular books. The stories reprinted in this omnibus edition chronicle the formation of the team, faceoffs with the assassin Deathstroke and the Fearsome Five, a misguided confrontation with the Justice League and a battle royal against Trigon, a demon who is also Raven’s father. About midway in there is a “day in the life” story that focused on the civilian lives of the heroes. That issue cemented this series as doing something different: the creative team was developing three-dimensional characters and exploring new directions.

docs.lead_paragraph: A phenomenally wealthy Indian who excites hostility and suspicion is an unusual creature, a fish that has managed to muddy the waters it swims in. The glow of admiration lighting up the rich and the successful disperses before it reaches him, hinting that things have gone wrong somewhere. It suggests that beneath the sleek coating of luxury, deep under the sheen of power, there is a failure barely sensed by the man who owns that failure along with his expensive accoutrements. This was Arindam Chaudhuri’s situation when I first met him in 2007. He had achieved great wealth and prominence, partly by projecting an image of himself as wealthy and prominent. Yet somewhere along the way he had also created the opposite effect, which – in spite of his best efforts – had given him a reputation as a fraud, scamster and Johnny-come-lately.

docs.lead_paragraph: WHEN the impresario Serge Diaghilev died in 1929, the Ballets Russes — the company he had formed in 1909 — folded with him. The sense of loss was so abysslike that in the years that followed several new companies around the Western world (some also bearing the name Ballets Russes) were established to recapture his achievement. Still, much had been lost. Some of his most celebrated dancers retired at once or soon after. Only one of his five choreographers (George Balanchine) went on — eventually — to bigger and better things. Seldom since then has ballet had the same force as a vehicle for the new.

docs.snippet: I met Cliff Levy for the first time when he was in New York to collect his Pulitzer last spring. He came up to my office and pitched the story that’s in this week’s magazine, about how he put his three Brooklyn-bred kids in a Russian school, even ...
docs.lead_paragraph: I met Cliff Levy for the first time when he was in New York to collect his Pulitzer Prize last spring. He came up to my office and pitched a story about how he put his three Brooklyn-bred kids in a Russian school, even though they didn’t speak the language, when he was sent to Moscow as a correspondent for The Times. I could hardly say yes fast enough to his story, which I knew would fascinate the many people on this earth obsessed with how best to educate their children. But I also privately wondered if maybe Cliff wasn’t a little insane. I have twin daughters who just started kindergarten this week, and though their school could not be a warmer, more welcoming place — they even speak English there! — I still worry about their adjustment to an unfamiliar environment.

docs.snippet: A look at the art installations associated with the Toronto International Film Festival, including one by the actor James Franco.
docs.lead_paragraph: TORONTO — It is increasingly de rigeur for film festivals to encompass much more than film. Many major festivals now supplement screenings with installations and performances, and entire sections are devoted to exploring the intersection of cinema and the other arts. The Rotterdam Film Festival pioneered this kind of cross-disciplinary programming in the ’90s. Berlin has an annual Forum Expanded mini-festival, which spills logically into the museums and galleries of an art-centric city. Sundance has a New Frontier sidebar. And since 2007 the Toronto International Film Festival has made room for film-based art installations in the Future Projections program.

headline.main: James Franco and Other Art Stars of the Toronto Film Festival

docs.lead_paragraph: Deganit Shemy & Company’s “2 kilos of sea” began life last year as a short, site-specific piece for two men and four women in a concrete churchyard near City Hall. During its move inside to the Baryshnikov Arts Center, the dance has expanded a little, shed a man, swapped two women and acquired a set. Lenore Doxsee has partitioned the stage with bright orange plastic netting and patches of fake grass. The artificial environment plays an important role, particularly the photo backdrop (of an empty pool) behind which the dancers can hide. But the work is now less about architecture and more about story.

docs.snippet: Edi & the Wolf brings Austrian cuisine to a not-entirely-gentrified stretch of Avenue C, and recently, two Austrians and a German had a “schnitzel craving.”
docs.lead_paragraph: When Eduard Frauneder and Wolfgang Ban brought their brand of seasonal Austrian cooking down to a not-entirely-gentrified stretch of Avenue C near Seventh Street last December, many of their fans from the commissary at the German Mission to the United Nations and their high-end restaurant Seäsonal in Midtown followed along. As a result, on any given evening or weekend afternoon, Edi & the Wolf plays host to a mix of funky young Lower East Siders and buttoned-down diplomats. The room and its enclosed garden out back are fashioned after a Viennese wine tavern, with wood reclaimed from church benches, a church bell rope draped over the bar and a confessional bench in one of the bathrooms. On Tuesday night at Table 1, just inside the door, two Austrians and a German discussed travel and the anticipated street snarls when the world’s leaders flood the city for the meeting of the United Nations General Assembly this week. DIANE CARDWELL

headline.main: Where Diplomats and Young East Siders Collide

So when my younger brother and his wife announced their first pregnancy, I — then in my mid-30s — listened hopefully for that famous tick-tock, and when it didn’t sound, slunk back to my familiar unknown. My indecision, I was forced to accept, was fast reaching its expiration date. And then on a bright March afternoon I entered a hushed delivery room, and my brother handed me a small white bundle, and I felt something, not maternal exactly, but decidedly formidable: a primal pull, a plummet. docs.lead_paragraph: The Inter-American Court on Human Rights ruled on Friday that Venezuela must allow Leopoldo López, a prominent opposition leader, to run for public office. The decision could shake up a presidential election scheduled for October 2012, opening the way for a strong opponent to run against President Hugo Chávez. Mr. López, a former mayor of Chacao, a municipality in Caracas, was disqualified by Mr. Chávez’s government from running because of legal claims against him from his time as mayor. Mr. López argued that the disqualification, a method used by Venezuela’s government against other opposition figures, amounted to political discrimination. In a statement, the Foreign Ministry called the ruling “politically partial.” Venezuela is believed to be required to respect the decision by the court, a judicial entity of the Organization of American States.

docs.lead_paragraph: Britain has altered a law to make it more difficult for private citizens and activist groups to seek the arrest of foreign politicians for crimes like torture, genocide and war crimes. The change, which took effect Thursday, means that Israeli officials who had feared traveling to Britain because of threats that they might be arrested will now be able to visit again. Under the old law, people could apply to magistrates to have arrest warrants issued against people suspected of committing crimes against humanity. But now the director of public prosecutions will have to consent before such arrest warrants can be issued. The law has been a bone of contention between Israel and Britain for some time, after former Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni canceled a trip to Britain amid reports that activists would seek to have her arrested in connection with the Gaza offensive in 2008 and 2009.

docs.snippet: A defunct, six-ton NASA satellite will plummet out of orbit in about a week. The falling satellite, was launched in 1991 from the space shuttle Discovery to study the dynamics and chemistry of the upper atmosphere.
docs.lead_paragraph: A defunct, six-ton NASA satellite will plummet out of orbit in about a week — on Sept. 23, give or take a day. But where it will land nobody knows. The orbit of the Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite passes over latitudes as far north as Edinburgh and as far south as Cape Town, and the trail of debris will stretch to about 500 miles long. NASA puts the chances that anything would hit anyone at 1 in 3,200 and notes that there are no known cases of injury by falling satellite, not even when its Skylab space station crashed into western Australia in 1979. The falling satellite, about one-tenth the mass of Skylab, was launched in 1991 from the space shuttle Discovery to study the dynamics and chemistry of the upper atmosphere and was decommissioned in 2005 when its fuel ran out and its batteries failed.

headline.main: Satellite to Land, Somewhere

docs.abstract: History has shown that though science is fallible, it will do better than any other approach at getting things right.
docs.snippet: History has shown that though science is fallible, it will do better than any other approach at getting things right.
docs.lead_paragraph: Naturalism is the philosophical theory that treats science as our most reliable source of knowledge and scientific method as the most effective route to knowledge. In a recent essay for The Stone, Timothy Williamson correctly reports that naturalism is popular in philosophy. In fact it is now a dominant approach in several areas of philosophy — ethics, epistemology, the philosophy of mind, philosophy of science and, most of in all, metaphysics, the study of the basic constituents of reality. Metaphysics is important: if it turns out that reality contains only the kinds of things that hard science recognizes, the implications will be grave for what we value in human experience.

headline.main: Why I Am a Naturalist

docs.abstract: In the great pizza wars of New York City, Ray’s Pizza, opened by a man named Ralph in 1959, was the original that was so original it did not have the word “original” in its name.
docs.snippet: In the great pizza wars of New York City, Ray’s Pizza, opened by a man named Ralph in 1959, was the original that was so original it did not have the word “original” in its name.
docs.lead_paragraph: It did not call itself the flagship Ray’s Pizza because it never really had a fleet. It was not Original Ray’s or Famous Ray’s or Original Famous Ray’s or Real Ray’s or Ray’s on Ice or any of the other cloned shops sprinkled like shredded mozzarella all over town. It was simply Ray’s Pizza, and in the great pizza wars of New York City, it was respected as having been the first, standing more or less above the fray at 27 Prince Street in Little Italy, with tree limbs holding up the basement ceiling and an owner whose name wasn’t even Ray.

headline.main: Ray’s Pizza, the First of Many, Counts Down to Its Last Slice

docs.lead_paragraph: Take a 17-year-old animated movie, gussy it up with 3-D visuals, and give it a two-week stunt release in theaters when competition from other family films is weak. Presto: “The Lion King” roars again. This Walt Disney Studios movie, which sold $1.2 billion at the global box office in 1994 (after adjusting for inflation), was No. 1 over the weekend with an estimated $29.3 million in ticket sales, a result that significantly exceeded expectations. Second place went to “Contagion,” the Warner Brothers-Participant Media disease thriller; it took in about $14.5 million for a two-week total of $44.2 million, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles box office data. The violent crime drama “Drive” (FilmDistrict) was third with about $11 million, while “The Help” (DreamWorks Studios) was in fourth place, taking in $6.4 million for a six week total of $147.4 million. Rounding out the top five was a remake of “Straw Dogs” (Sony Pictures Entertainment) that sold an estimated $5 million in tickets.

headline.main: Now in 3-D, ‘Lion King’ Returns to Lead at Box Office
